questions.q: You save a file in nano and then exit. Which sequence of shortcuts does that correctly?
choices: Ctrl+X to save, then Ctrl+O to exit.
Ctrl+S to save, then Ctrl+Q to exit.
Ctrl+W to save, then Ctrl+X to exit.
Ctrl+O then Enter to save, then Ctrl+X to exit.
questions.explain: In nano the workflow is: Ctrl+O (Write Out) to save, press Enter to confirm the filename, then Ctrl+X to exit. Ctrl+S is not a nano shortcut, and Ctrl+W opens the search bar.

questions.q: You run ls -l and see the permission string -rw-r--r-- on a file. What can the file's group members do with it?
choices: Read the file only.
Read and write the file, but not execute it.
Read, write, and execute the file.
Nothing — they have no permissions at all.
questions.explain: The 10-character string breaks down as: file type (-), owner permissions (rw-), group permissions (r--), others permissions (r--). The group section r-- means read only — no write, no execute.

questions.q: You delete a file with the rm command in the terminal. Where does it go?
choices: It moves to a hidden .trash folder you can restore it from.
It is compressed and stored in /var/log until the next reboot.
It is gone immediately and permanently — there is no undo.
It is moved to /tmp and wiped only when you restart the Pi.
questions.explain: The Linux terminal has no Recycle Bin. rm removes files instantly and permanently. /tmp is scratch space that is cleared on reboot, but rm does not send files there — it simply deletes them.

questions.q: What is the difference between the cp and mv commands?
choices: cp moves a file permanently; mv makes a temporary copy that disappears on reboot.
cp and mv do the same thing — both rename the file in place.
cp removes the original file after copying; mv keeps the original in place.
cp leaves the original file in place and creates a duplicate; mv removes the original from its current location.
questions.explain: cp (copy) leaves the source file where it is and creates a new copy. mv (move/rename) removes the file from its current location and places it at the destination — or simply renames it if the destination is the same folder.

questions.q: What does the sudo command do when placed before another command?
choices: It permanently switches your session to the root account for the rest of the terminal window.
It asks the root user to approve the command before it runs.
It runs just that one command with full root privileges, then your account returns to normal.
It backs up any files that will be changed before the command runs.
questions.explain: sudo (superuser do) grants root-level power for a single command only. Once that command finishes, your session is back to the normal pi account. To stay as root for multiple commands you would need sudo -i, which the chapter warns beginners to avoid.
